mean: to teach each student according to their ability
lit: to give teaching according to the material (each person's talent)

story.text: Two of Confucius's disciples asked him the same question: when I hear something right, should I act on it at once? He told the bold Zilu to consult his father and elder brothers first, but told the hesitant Ran You to act at once. When another disciple asked why the answers differed, Confucius said Ran You holds back, so he pushed him forward, while Zilu rushes ahead, so he held him back.

use.how: Used as a predicate about teachers, parents or coaches: 老师要因材施教。 It takes no object; say 对学生因材施教.

near.diff: 对症下药 fits a remedy to a problem; 因材施教 fits teaching to the person being taught.

cue: A teacher gently encourages the shy pupil and gives the overconfident one harder challenges, each according to who they are.

ctx.s: 好老师懂得{因材施教}，不会用同一种方法教所有学生。
ctx.en: A good teacher knows how to teach each student differently, rather than using one method for everyone.

ctx.s: 这两个孩子性格完全不同，你得{因材施教}才行。
ctx.en: These two children have completely different personalities; you have to teach each in their own way.

ctx.s: 学校推行小班教学，就是为了更好地{因材施教}。
ctx.en: The school introduced small classes precisely so it could better teach each student according to their ability.

ctx.s: “为什么他的作业和我的不一样？”“老师这是在{因材施教}。”
ctx.en: "Why is his homework different from mine?" "The teacher is fitting the work to each of you."

ctx.s: 这位教练{因材施教}，给每个队员定了不同的训练计划。
ctx.en: The coach tailored his teaching to each player and gave everyone a different training plan.

ctx.s: 学习软件根据测试结果给每个人推荐不同的课程，也算是一种{因材施教}。
ctx.en: The learning app recommends different lessons to each user based on their test results, which is a kind of teaching to the individual.

bad.s: 这家餐厅{因材施教}，菜做得很好。
bad.en: (meant: the restaurant makes good use of its ingredients)
bad.why: The 'material' here is a person's talent: the idiom is only about teaching people, never about cooking or using ingredients.

bad.s: 我请了一位家教来{因材施教}我。
bad.en: (meant: I hired a tutor to teach me individually)
bad.why: It takes no direct object. Name the learner with a preposition instead: the tutor teaches 'towards me' (dui wo) according to my ability.

mean: to tailor the remedy to the actual problem
lit: to prescribe medicine that matches the illness

story.text: Two officials came to the physician Hua Tuo with the same complaint: headache and fever. He gave one a medicine to purge him and the other a medicine to make him sweat. When someone questioned the different treatments, Hua Tuo explained that the two illnesses had different causes, so they had to be treated differently. By the next morning both men were well.

use.how: Used as a predicate, often after 要, 才能 or 必须, about solving any problem by first finding its real cause: 找到原因才能对症下药。

near.diff: 因材施教 is about teaching people according to their ability; 对症下药 is about choosing a fix that matches the cause of a problem.

cue: Sales fell because deliveries were slow, not because of price, so the manager fixes delivery instead of cutting prices.

ctx.s: 医生先给病人做了检查，然后{对症下药}。
ctx.en: The doctor examined the patient first and then prescribed the right treatment.

ctx.s: 想解决问题，先要找到原因，才能{对症下药}。
ctx.en: To solve a problem you must find its cause first; only then can you apply the right fix.

ctx.s: 你连问题出在哪儿都不知道，怎么{对症下药}？
ctx.en: You don't even know where the problem lies, so how can you find the right remedy?

ctx.s: 销量下降是因为送货太慢，我们应该{对症下药}，而不是一味打广告。
ctx.en: Sales dropped because delivery is too slow; we should fix that, not just keep advertising.

ctx.s: 市里针对堵车的主要原因{对症下药}，新开了几条公交线路。
ctx.en: The city targeted the main cause of the traffic jams and opened several new bus routes.

ctx.s: 这份报告分析得很透彻，提出的办法也称得上{对症下药}。
ctx.en: The report's analysis is thorough, and the measures it proposes really go to the root of the problem.

bad.s: 我感冒了，去药店{对症下药}了一盒感冒药。
bad.en: (meant: I went to the pharmacy and bought cold medicine)
bad.why: It does not mean buying medicine and takes no object; it means choosing a remedy that fits the cause.

bad.s: 这个方案{对症下药}，根本没解决问题。
bad.en: (meant: the plan missed the point and solved nothing)
bad.why: The idiom says the remedy fits the cause, so it contradicts 'solved nothing'. To say a plan misses the cause, negate it.

lit: to gather thoughts and widen the benefit

story.text: Zhuge Liang, chancellor of the state of Shu, wrote to his officials that the reason they shared in running the government was to gather the thoughts of many and widen the benefit of loyal advice. He asked them to speak up and argue with him whenever they disagreed, rather than simply going along.

use.how: Used as a predicate, usually with 大家 as subject, when a group is asked for suggestions: 我们开个会，大家集思广益。

near.diff: 群策群力 is everyone contributing both plans and effort to get something done; 集思广益 is gathering many people's ideas and advice.

cue: The team is stuck on a name for a new product, so the boss calls everyone together to throw out suggestions.

ctx.s: 这个问题我一个人想不出来，大家{集思广益}吧。
ctx.en: I can't figure this out on my own; let's all put our heads together.

ctx.s: 公司开了个会，请员工{集思广益}，给新产品起名字。
ctx.en: The company held a meeting and asked staff to pool their ideas for naming the new product.

ctx.s: 我们设了一个意见箱，目的就是{集思广益}。
ctx.en: We set up a suggestion box precisely to gather everyone's ideas.

ctx.s: “下周的活动怎么安排？”“别急，周一开会，大家{集思广益}。”
ctx.en: "How should we plan next week's event?" "Don't worry, we'll meet on Monday and all chip in ideas."

ctx.s: 这份计划是全组{集思广益}的结果，不是哪一个人的功劳。
ctx.en: This plan came out of the whole group pooling its ideas; it isn't one person's credit.

ctx.s: 遇到难题时，{集思广益}往往比一个人苦想更有效。
ctx.en: When facing a hard problem, pooling ideas often works better than one person racking their brain.

bad.s: 我一个人在家{集思广益}，想了一个好办法。
bad.en: (meant: I thought hard by myself at home and came up with a good idea)
bad.why: It needs many people contributing ideas; one person thinking alone at home has nothing to pool.

bad.s: 他很{集思广益}，什么都知道。
bad.en: (meant: he is very knowledgeable)
bad.why: It is an action a group takes, not an adjective for a well-informed person, and it cannot follow 'very'.

mean: knowing both oneself and one's opponent
lit: know yourself, know the other side

story.text: In the chapter on planning attacks, Sun Tzu writes: if you know the enemy and know yourself, you will not be in danger in a hundred battles; if you know yourself but not the enemy, you will win one and lose one; if you know neither, you will be in danger in every battle. Sun Tzu's order is 'know the other, know yourself'; today the idiom usually puts oneself first and is quoted with 'not in danger in a hundred battles'.

use.how: Used as a predicate or quoted as advice before any contest, exam, negotiation or interview, often as 知己知彼，百战不殆.

near.diff: 有自知之明 is only knowing your own limits; 知己知彼 always involves a rival or opponent as well.

cue: Before the final, the coach makes the team study both their own weak spots and the other side's match videos.

ctx.s: 比赛前先看看对手的录像，{知己知彼}嘛。
ctx.en: Watch the opponent's videos before the match; you need to know them as well as yourself.

ctx.s: {知己知彼}，百战不殆，谈判前一定要做好调查。
ctx.en: Know yourself and your opponent and you'll never be at risk; do your research before negotiating.

ctx.s: “你为什么一直在研究对手的价格？”“{知己知彼}才能赢啊。”
ctx.en: "Why do you keep studying your competitor's prices?" "You can only win if you know them and yourself."

ctx.s: 面试前，他既整理了自己的长处，也研究了这家公司，算是{知己知彼}。
ctx.en: Before the interview he listed his own strengths and researched the company, so he knew both sides.

ctx.s: 教练要求队员既分析自己的弱点，也研究对方的打法，做到{知己知彼}。
ctx.en: The coach had the players analyse their own weaknesses and study the other team's style, so they knew both.

ctx.s: 这本讲商业竞争的书，核心就是{知己知彼}这四个字。
ctx.en: This book on business competition comes down to four characters: know yourself and know your rival.

bad.s: 我们俩是{知己知彼}的好朋友。
bad.en: (meant: we are close friends who understand each other)
bad.why: Here zhiji is not the noun 'close friend' but 'know oneself'; the idiom is about knowing an opponent, not about friendship.

bad.s: 他很{知己知彼}，知道自己适合当老师。
bad.en: (meant: he is self-aware and knows he suits teaching)
bad.why: There is no rival here, and it is not an adjective after 'very'. Knowing only your own limits is a different idiom.

lit: in the circumstances there is something that can be pardoned

use.how: Used as a predicate about a mistake or wrong act that has a mitigating reason: 迟到是不对，但情有可原。 It admits the act was wrong.

near.diff: 无可厚非 says something hardly deserves criticism at all; 情有可原 admits it was wrong but finds a reason to excuse it.

cue: An employee missed a deadline, but only because his child was in hospital that week. How do you judge the lapse?

ctx.s: 他第一次做这种工作，出点错也{情有可原}。
ctx.en: It's his first time doing this kind of work, so a few mistakes are understandable.

ctx.s: 孩子是饿坏了才偷吃点心的，{情有可原}，别骂他了。
ctx.en: The child only sneaked the snacks because he was starving; it's forgivable, so don't scold him.

ctx.s: 迟到是不对，不过路上出了车祸，这就{情有可原}了。
ctx.en: Being late is wrong, but there was a car accident on the way, so it can be excused.

ctx.s: “她那天为什么发那么大的火？”“她刚失去亲人，{情有可原}。”
ctx.en: "Why did she lose her temper like that?" "She had just lost a family member; it's understandable."

ctx.s: 法官认为被告的行为{情有可原}，判得比较轻。
ctx.en: The judge found the defendant's actions excusable in the circumstances and gave a lighter sentence.

ctx.s: 新手犯错{情有可原}，可同样的错犯三次就说不过去了。
ctx.en: A beginner's mistake can be excused, but making the same one three times can't.

bad.s: 你帮了我这么大的忙，真是{情有可原}。
bad.en: (meant: you have been so kind to me)
bad.why: It excuses a wrong act; helping someone is not wrong and needs no excuse. Just thank the person.

bad.s: 老板{情有可原}了我的错误。
bad.en: (meant: the boss forgave my mistake)
bad.why: It is not a verb meaning 'forgive' and takes no object; it describes the wrong act itself as excusable.

lit: the chief of the crime, the head of the disaster

use.how: A noun, usually in ……是……的罪魁祸首. Said of a person or of a thing blamed for harm: 熬夜是失眠的罪魁祸首。 Light, joking use is common.

near.diff: 始作俑者 is whoever first started a bad practice that others followed; 罪魁祸首 is the main one to blame for a harm.

cue: Every computer in the office crashed, and it turns out one virus-infected USB stick was behind it all. What was the stick?

ctx.s: 原来，打碎花瓶的{罪魁祸首}是家里的猫。
ctx.en: It turned out the culprit who broke the vase was our cat.

ctx.s: “谁把蛋糕吃光了？”“{罪魁祸首}就站在你面前。”
ctx.en: "Who ate all the cake?" "The guilty party is standing right in front of you."

ctx.s: 长期熬夜是他身体变差的{罪魁祸首}。
ctx.en: Staying up late night after night is the main reason his health got worse.

ctx.s: 专家指出，汽车尾气是城市空气污染的{罪魁祸首}之一。
ctx.en: Experts point out that car exhaust is one of the chief culprits behind urban air pollution.

ctx.s: 警方调查了一个月，终于抓到了这起诈骗案的{罪魁祸首}。
ctx.en: After a month of investigation, the police finally caught the mastermind of the fraud.

ctx.s: 公司亏损，大家都怪市场不好，其实管理混乱才是{罪魁祸首}。
ctx.en: Everyone blames the market for the company's losses, but chaotic management is the real culprit.

bad.s: 他是这次比赛的{罪魁祸首}，帮球队拿了冠军。
bad.en: (meant: he was the key player who won the title)
bad.why: It always assigns blame for harm, never credit. A player who won the title is a hero, not a culprit.

bad.s: 他{罪魁祸首}了这场事故。
bad.en: (meant: he caused this accident)
bad.why: It is a noun, not a verb. Say that he is the chief culprit of the accident, using the pattern shi ... de.

mean: to put the trivial before the essential
lit: to turn the root and the branch tips upside down

use.how: Used as a predicate, often after 就, 有点 or 这不是……吗, to criticise wrong priorities: 只顾装修不管产品，就本末倒置了。

near.diff: 舍本逐末 stresses abandoning the essential to chase the trivial; 本末倒置 stresses getting the order of importance backwards.
因小失大 is about a real loss caused by caring about something small; 本末倒置 is about misjudging what matters most.

cue: A café spends its money on fancy decor and online ads while its coffee keeps getting worse.

ctx.s: 为了减肥连饭都不吃，把身体搞坏了，这就{本末倒置}了。
ctx.en: Skipping meals to lose weight until you ruin your health is getting your priorities backwards.

ctx.s: 他花一晚上装饰笔记本，却一个单词也没背，这不是{本末倒置}吗？
ctx.en: He spent the whole evening decorating his notebook and didn't learn a single word; isn't that backwards?

ctx.s: 开店最重要的是产品，装修只是陪衬，你却把装修当成重点，这就{本末倒置}了。
ctx.en: In running a shop the product matters most and the decor is secondary; treating the decor as the main thing gets it backwards.

ctx.s: 学车是为了安全驾驶，只想着背考题，有点{本末倒置}。
ctx.en: You learn to drive in order to drive safely; just memorising test answers is rather missing the point.

ctx.s: “我加班是为了让家人过得好。”“可你一年见不到孩子几次，不觉得{本末倒置}吗？”
ctx.en: "I work overtime for my family's sake." "But you barely see your kids all year; don't you think that's backwards?"

ctx.s: 这家公司把大部分预算花在宣传上，产品质量却越来越差，可谓{本末倒置}。
ctx.en: The company spends most of its budget on promotion while its products get worse; its priorities are upside down.

bad.s: 他把书架上的书都{本末倒置}了。
bad.en: (meant: he put the books on the shelf upside down)
bad.why: It is not about physically turning objects over; it criticises getting priorities in the wrong order.

bad.s: 这个故事的结局{本末倒置}，非常精彩。
bad.en: (meant: the story's ending had a brilliant twist)
bad.why: It criticises wrong priorities; it is not praise for a surprising plot reversal and cannot be called brilliant.

mean: to lose something big for a small gain
lit: because of the small, to lose the big

use.how: Used as a predicate, often as a warning (别因小失大) or a verdict after the loss (真是因小失大). Said of choices that save a little and cost a lot.

near.diff: 得不偿失 says the gain is worth less than the cost; 因小失大 says caring about a minor thing made you lose an important one.

cue: To save a little on a cheap flight, she booked one that landed after her job interview had already begun.

ctx.s: 为了省一点钱买便宜的头盔，可别{因小失大}。
ctx.en: Don't buy a cheap helmet to save a little money and end up losing far more.

ctx.s: 做生意要看长远，不能为了眼前的小利{因小失大}。
ctx.en: In business you have to think long term, not lose something big for a quick small profit.

ctx.s: “这点小病不用去医院吧？”“拖久了可能更严重，别{因小失大}。”
ctx.en: "It's only a small illness, no need for the hospital, right?" "It could get worse if you wait; don't save a little trouble now and pay for it later."

ctx.s: 为了跟客户争几块钱的运费，他丢了整个订单，真是{因小失大}！
ctx.en: He argued with the client over a few yuan of shipping and lost the whole order. What a false economy!

ctx.s: 考试时他在一道小题上花了半小时，后面的大题都没做完，{因小失大}。
ctx.en: In the exam he spent half an hour on one small question and couldn't finish the big ones after it.

ctx.s: 他为了一点加班费天天熬夜，把最要紧的健康赔了进去，这是典型的{因小失大}。
ctx.en: He stayed up every night for a little overtime pay and sacrificed what matters most, his health: a classic case of losing much for little.

bad.s: 他从小职员一步步做到了总经理，真是{因小失大}。
bad.en: (meant: he rose from a junior clerk to general manager)
bad.why: It describes a loss caused by chasing a small gain, not rising step by step from a small post to a big one.

bad.s: 我们输了一场小组赛，却赢了总冠军，真是{因小失大}。
bad.en: (meant: we lost a small match but won the big title)
bad.why: This reverses it: the idiom means losing the big thing. Here you gained the big thing, so it does not fit.

mean: having nothing to be ashamed of
lit: to question one's heart and find no shame

use.how: Used as a predicate, mostly about oneself: 我问心无愧。 Said of one's conduct when facing doubt or a bad outcome; also 对……问心无愧.

near.diff: 心安理得 is simply feeling at ease, often said critically of someone who should not; 问心无愧 claims one truly did nothing wrong.

cue: Accused of cheating, a student who really earned her grade says her conscience is completely clear.

ctx.s: 我已经尽了全力，结果怎样都{问心无愧}。
ctx.en: I have done my very best, so whatever the result, I have nothing to reproach myself for.

ctx.s: 别人怎么说我不管，我做事{问心无愧}。
ctx.en: I don't care what others say; my conscience is clear about how I act.

ctx.s: “你真的没动过那份文件？”“没有，我{问心无愧}。”
ctx.en: "You really didn't touch that file?" "No. My conscience is clear."

ctx.s: 做生意不骗人，虽然赚得少一点，但{问心无愧}。
ctx.en: If you don't cheat people in business you may earn a bit less, but your conscience is clear.

ctx.s: 当了三十年医生，她说自己对每个病人都{问心无愧}。
ctx.en: After thirty years as a doctor, she says she has nothing to be ashamed of towards any patient.

ctx.s: 项目虽然失败了，可他觉得自己每一步都{问心无愧}，并不后悔。
ctx.en: Although the project failed, he felt he had nothing to be ashamed of at any step and had no regrets.

bad.s: 他做了那么多坏事，却一点也{问心无愧}。
bad.en: (meant: he did so many bad things and felt no shame at all)
bad.why: The idiom means one really did nothing wrong. Someone at ease after doing wrong is shameless, which is a different idea.

bad.s: 这次考试我考了满分，太{问心无愧}了！
bad.en: (meant: I got full marks and I'm so proud!)
bad.why: It is about a clear conscience over one's conduct, not pride in a good result, and it does not take 'so very'.

lit: what meets the eye startles the heart

use.how: Used as a predicate or attributive (触目惊心的画面) to describe a disturbing sight: wounds, ruins, pollution, alarming figures. It describes the sight, not the person.

near.diff: 惊心动魄 is thrilling and heart-pounding, as in a match or adventure; 触目惊心 is a disturbing sight of damage or harm.

cue: Volunteers arrive at a beach and find it buried under heaps of plastic waste and dead fish.

ctx.s: 地震过后，街道上一片废墟，{触目惊心}。
ctx.en: After the earthquake the streets were in ruins, a shocking sight.

ctx.s: 他腿上的伤口又深又长，看起来{触目惊心}。
ctx.en: The wound on his leg was deep and long, horrifying to look at.

ctx.s: “你看到那段车祸视频了吗？”“看了，真是{触目惊心}。”
ctx.en: "Did you see that car crash video?" "I did. It was really disturbing to watch."

ctx.s: 海滩上堆满了塑料垃圾，那画面让人{触目惊心}。
ctx.en: The beach was piled with plastic waste; the sight was shocking.

ctx.s: 报告中的数据{触目惊心}：每年都有大片森林消失。
ctx.en: The figures in the report are alarming: huge areas of forest disappear every year.

ctx.s: 这些照片记录了洪水过后的村庄，每一张都{触目惊心}。
ctx.en: These photos record the villages after the flood, and every one of them is distressing to see.

bad.s: 烟花太美了，让人{触目惊心}。
bad.en: (meant: the fireworks were stunningly beautiful)
bad.why: It is only for disturbing sights of harm or danger, never for something beautiful.

bad.s: 电话里听到这个消息，我{触目惊心}。
bad.en: (meant: I was shocked to hear the news on the phone)
bad.why: Its first half means 'meeting the eye', so it fits sights, not news heard; and it describes the sight, not the person.
